meta.title: A Recession Isn't Officially Declared The Way Most People Think
meta.hook: Most people think a recession needs two straight quarters of shrinking GDP. That's not actually the rule.
meta.description: The common rule of thumb, two consecutive quarters of falling GDP, isn't the official US definition. Recessions are actually dated by the National Bureau of Economic Research, a private nonprofit, which looks at a broader mix of measures including employment, income, and spending before making a call, sometimes months after a downturn has already started. Educational content only, not financial advice.

scenes.narration: Most people think a recession needs two straight quarters of shrinking GDP. That's not actually the rule.

visual.visual_intent: A red declining chart line on a dark financial screen, sharp and stark, cinematic
visual.decision_reason: hook: corrects the common rule of thumb

scenes.narration: In the US, recessions are officially dated by a group called the NBER. Not the government, a private nonprofit.

visual.visual_intent: A small committee seated around a table reviewing documents, muted office light, documentary tone
visual.decision_reason: NBER is the official, well-documented US recession-dating body

scenes.narration: They look at a broader mix. Employment, income, spending, industrial output, all at once.

visual.visual_intent: Several overlapping data charts on one dark screen, layered financial graphic

scenes.narration: Not just GDP. And not just two quarters.

visual.visual_intent: A calendar with two quarters crossed out, symbolic correction, minimal graphic

scenes.narration: Which means the call sometimes comes months after a downturn already started, once the fuller data is in.

visual.visual_intent: Calendar pages turning forward, symbolic of delay, warm desk light, cinematic
visual.decision_reason: the well-documented dating lag of NBER announcements

scenes.narration: The rule of thumb is a shortcut. The real definition is slower, and more careful. Follow for more.
